points.title: Cause, conséquence et condition dans l'argumentation
points.explanationEn:
Building a rigorous argument — the kind expected in a debate about climate policy or scientific evidence — means being precise about the logical relationship between your claims: is this a stated fact you're building from, an intended goal, an actual result, or a condition your conclusion depends on? French marks these distinctions not just with different connectors but, crucially, with different verb moods, and getting the mood wrong actively changes what you're claiming, not just how elegantly you're claiming it.

Étant donné que ('given that') introduces a fact you're treating as settled and building an argument on top of — it is always followed by the indicative, because by using it you are asserting the following clause as true, not hedging it: 'Étant donné que les températures augmentent, les glaciers reculent.' It behaves similarly to puisque and vu que, and is a staple opener for the premise of a scientific or policy argument.

De sorte que ('so that' / 'with the result that') is genuinely ambiguous in a way that rewards careful attention: it takes the indicative when it reports an actual, already-realized consequence, and the subjunctive when it expresses an intended purpose or desired outcome that hasn't necessarily happened yet. 'Le gouvernement a renforcé les normes, de sorte que les émissions ont baissé' (indicative — this baisse actually occurred; you're reporting a real result) contrasts with 'Il faut renforcer les normes de sorte que les émissions baissent' (subjunctive — the baisse is the hoped-for goal of the action, not a confirmed fact yet). English 'so that' doesn't force you to make this distinction, which is exactly why it's easy to default to the wrong mood in French. A related, more explicitly purpose-flavored variant is de sorte à ce que (a blend of de sorte à + à ce que, functionally close to de manière à ce que), which always takes the subjunctive because it exclusively expresses intended purpose: 'Les chercheurs ont reformulé le protocole de sorte à ce que les résultats soient reproductibles.'

Condition and restriction are handled by à condition que and à moins que, both of which require the subjunctive because a condition or an exception is, by definition, not yet a confirmed fact — it's a hypothetical that the main clause's truth depends on. À condition que ('provided that') sets a necessary condition: 'Le projet sera financé à condition que les études d'impact soient concluantes.' À moins que ('unless') introduces an exception that would block the main claim: 'La biodiversité continuera de décliner, à moins qu'on ne prenne des mesures urgentes.' Notice the ne in that last example — this is the ne explétif, a 'expletive' ne that carries no negative meaning on its own (the clause is not actually negated; adding pas would be a real, different negation). The ne explétif shows up optionally after à moins que, avant que, and a handful of other expressions of fear or apprehension, mostly in formal written register — it's a stylistic residue of Latin syntax, not a logical negative, so don't let it fool you into misreading the sentence's polarity.

examples.fr: Étant donné que les glaciers fondent plus vite chaque année, les experts s'inquiètent de la hausse du niveau des mers.
examples.en: Given that glaciers are melting faster every year, experts are worried about rising sea levels.
examples.note: Étant donné que + indicative: stated as an accepted fact.

examples.fr: Le gouvernement a investi massivement dans les énergies renouvelables, de sorte que les émissions ont chuté de 15 %.
examples.en: The government invested heavily in renewable energy, with the result that emissions dropped 15%.
examples.note: De sorte que + indicative: a realized, confirmed result.

examples.fr: Il faut réduire notre consommation d'énergie de sorte que les objectifs climatiques soient atteints.
examples.en: We must reduce our energy consumption so that the climate targets are met.
examples.note: De sorte que + subjunctive: an intended, not-yet-achieved purpose.

examples.fr: Les chercheurs ont revu leur méthodologie de sorte à ce que l'étude soit reproductible.
examples.en: The researchers revised their methodology so that the study would be reproducible.
examples.note: De sorte à ce que + subjunctive: purpose-only variant.

examples.fr: Le financement du projet sera maintenu à condition que les résultats préliminaires soient concluants.
examples.en: The project's funding will continue provided that the preliminary results are conclusive.

examples.fr: Les récoltes resteront stables à moins qu'une sécheresse ne survienne cet été.
examples.en: Crop yields will remain stable unless a drought occurs this summer.
examples.note: À moins que + subjunctive, with the non-negating 'ne explétif'.

examples.fr: Étant donné que les données sont incomplètes, il est difficile de tirer des conclusions fermes.
examples.en: Given that the data is incomplete, it is difficult to draw firm conclusions.

examples.fr: L'accord ne sera signé qu'à condition que tous les pays membres l'approuvent.
examples.en: The agreement will only be signed provided that all member states approve it.

examples.fr: Nous continuerons de surveiller la situation, à moins que de nouvelles preuves ne changent notre analyse.
examples.en: We will keep monitoring the situation, unless new evidence changes our analysis.

examples.fr: L'usine a modernisé ses filtres de sorte que la pollution locale a nettement diminué.
examples.en: The factory modernized its filters, with the result that local pollution decreased significantly.
examples.note: Indicative again: an accomplished, measurable result, not a hoped-for goal.

commonMistakes: Using the indicative after à condition que or à moins que, forgetting that both introduce a hypothetical condition and therefore require the subjunctive.
Defaulting to the subjunctive after étant donné que by treating it like a hedge, when it actually asserts a fact and takes the indicative.
Using the indicative after de sorte que even when expressing an intended, not-yet-realized purpose, instead of switching to the subjunctive for that meaning.
Misreading the ne explétif after à moins que as a genuine negation, or mistakenly adding 'pas' to it and thereby changing the sentence's actual meaning.

Using 'de sorte que' + subjunctive when the subject of both clauses is the same, instead of switching to the simpler infinitive construction 'de sorte à' + infinitive (or 'de manière à' + infinitive), which is more natural when there's no subject change.
whyItTrips: English 'so that' covers both a realized result and an intended goal without any grammatical marker distinguishing them, so English speakers have no built-in cue that French requires switching mood (indicative vs subjunctive) depending on which meaning is intended.
The ne explétif looks exactly like the first half of the everyday negative marker ne...pas, so scanning for it triggers a false read of negation in a clause that is not actually negated.

English 'given that', 'provided that', and 'unless' all take perfectly ordinary indicative-feeling clauses, giving no signal that French sorts these connectors into a fact-based group (indicative) and a hypothetical-based group (subjunctive) that must be memorized connector by connector.
